title: The N-Queens Problem
excerpt: The standard demonstration of backtracking, and the standard lesson too: a better encoding beat a better search by a factor of three hundred before any pruning happened at all.
seoTitle: N-Queens Problem: Backtracking Solution Explained Step by Step
seoDescription: N-Queens with backtracking: why one queen per row shrinks the problem 300-fold, naming diagonals with row plus or minus column, a full annotated trace of the backtracks, and why 88 solutions means an over-eager prune.

content.text: Eight queens on a chessboard, none of them attacking another. A queen covers her whole row, her whole column and both diagonals, so eight of them on 64 squares is a tight fit. There are exactly 92 solutions, and the problem is the standard demonstration of backtracking for a good reason: the naive approach is hopeless and one good idea plus one cheap check makes it instant.
Before writing any code, the framing decides almost everything. The obvious statement of the problem is "choose 8 squares out of 64", which gives about 4.4 billion arrangements.

Now use something you know about the answer. Two queens in the same row always attack each other, so any valid solution has exactly one queen per row. That is not a heuristic, it is a fact about every solution, so restricting to it loses nothing.

Reframed, the question becomes "which column does each row's queen go in", which is 8 choices repeated 8 times: 16.7 million. Nearly three hundred times smaller, and it came from thinking rather than from code.

rows: One queen per row, choose its column
Reject attacked squares as you go
checking early instead of at the end

content.text: This generalizes past eight queens. Before reaching for a faster search, it is worth asking whether the representation itself can be made smaller, since a better encoding usually beats a better search.
With one queen per row, rows take care of themselves, columns are easy since you keep a set of used columns, and diagonals are the part that looks fiddly and turns out not to be.
Two squares are on the same "\\" diagonal exactly when
row - col
matches, and on the same "/" diagonal exactly when
row + col
matches. So each diagonal has a single number naming it, and checking a diagonal is a set lookup like the column check.

body.code:
row - col is constant down a "\" diagonal      row + col is constant down a "/" diagonal

     c0 c1 c2 c3                                   c0 c1 c2 c3
 r0   0  -1 -2 -3                              r0   0   1  2  3
 r1   1   0 -1 -2                              r1   1   2  3  4
 r2   2   1  0 -1                              r2   2   3  4  5
 r3   3   2  1  0                              r3   3   4  5  6

content.text: Three sets, three constant-time lookups, and a square is either safe or not. Without this you would scan the placed queens each time, which is fine at n = 8 and starts to hurt as the board grows.

Below is the search running on a 4 by 4 board. Use Step rather than Play, so each placement and backtrack gets its own moment instead of blurring past. Columns are lettered a to d, rows numbered 1 to 4, filling one row at a time from the top.

Watch what happens once queens are sitting on a1 and c2. Every column in row 3 is attacked, so the loop finishes having placed nothing and the call simply returns. That return is the backtrack. There is no special instruction for it, just a function running out of columns to try.

Keep watching after that, and the search eventually abandons row 1 entirely: once every arrangement starting with a queen on a1 has failed, it concludes nothing beginning there can work and moves on to b1. Twenty tries proved a single fact about the first row, and every one of them was necessary. Skip any of it and you risk throwing away a real solution along with the dead ends.
It reaches the first solution only after backing all the way out of the a1 branch and restarting from b1. Brute force over all 4-square placements would test 1,820 arrangements to get there.
Change the board size and watch the node counter. Between 6 and 8 the work grows quickly, and the difference between the pruned search and the raw arrangement count grows faster still.

variants.code:
def solve_n_queens(n):
    solutions, queen_in_row = [], []
    used_cols, used_down, used_up = set(), set(), set()

    def place(row):
        if row == n:
            solutions.append(queen_in_row[:])
            return

        for col in range(n):
            down, up = row - col, row + col
            if col in used_cols or down in used_down or up in used_up:
                continue

            used_cols.add(col); used_down.add(down); used_up.add(up)
            queen_in_row.append(col)

            place(row + 1)

            queen_in_row.pop()
            used_cols.discard(col); used_down.discard(down); used_up.discard(up)

    place(0)
    return solutions

content.text: Compare it against the template. The stopping test is
row === n
, the choices are the
n
columns of the current row, the prune is the three-set lookup, and the un-choose removes exactly what the choose added. Four pieces of state go up and four come back down.
The solution counts are worth having in front of you, partly as a check on your own implementation.

The dip at 6 is real and surprises people. There is no simple formula for these numbers, which is part of why the problem stayed interesting: for larger boards, counting the solutions is done by running a search rather than by evaluating an expression.

If your solver returns 88 rather than 92 on the 8 by 8 board, the search is not broken. A prune is rejecting placements that were actually legal, and the diagonal arithmetic is the first place to look.
Getting a diagonal formula backwards.
Using
row + col
for both diagonals is the classic slip. It runs, it produces fewer solutions than it should, and nothing looks wrong. Check against the table above.
Removing only some of the state on the way out.
Four things were added and all four must be removed. Missing one leaves a phantom queen blocking squares in sibling branches.
Checking safety after placing rather than before.
It works and it wastes the prune, since you build the state and then immediately tear it down.
Storing a reference to the working board is the same copying bug as everywhere else in this section, so take a snapshot when you record a solution.
